modern-skepticism-a-journey-through-the-:
Joseph Barker published this spiritual autobiography at Philadelphia in 1874. Its subtitle tells the arc: a trip through the land of doubt and back again. The first chapter tells his early life: entering the church, the ministry, and happy days. Then came a sad change, and Barker asks how it happened.

His second chapter catalogs the causes of unbelief. He names vice, inborn tendencies to doubt, and disappointed hopes. He also blames creeds that misrepresent Christ, church divisions, and ignorant defenders of the faith. False science completes his list. Barker, once a noted preacher turned skeptic, writes his return to faith as a cautionary life story.
mythology-of-aryan-nations-chowkhamba:
The Reverend George Cox wrote The Mythology of the Aryan Nations in the Victorian age. The Chowkhamba house in India later reprinted his survey. Cox was a clergyman drawn to the science of myth.

He compares tales from India, Persia, Greece, and the North. Sun heroes and dawn maidens recur in his scheme. Like many of his day, he read most myths as weather stories. That theory is dated now, yet the gathered tales retain value. The book shows comparative myth at its boldest, and why later scholars had to rebuild the field.
nasa-tm-19670003832-propellant-feed-duct:
P. L. Muller Jr., of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, describes the plumbing of the Saturn rockets in this memorandum. His subject is the ducting that carries liquid propellant from the tanks to the engines. He also covers the flexible lines that let the engines swivel, or gimbal, to steer the vehicle.

Muller describes the feed system concepts and layouts used on the Saturn V. For the gimbal lines, he traces the line of designs from the Jupiter vehicle through the Saturn I. The Saturn V systems are the most sophisticated in that line. He notes that future vehicles' feed systems will build on Saturn V work.

the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-0:
Sergius Sulpicius Galba opens the seventh volume of Suetonius's Lives, in the Thomson translation revised by T. Forester. Suetonius begins by declaring Nero the last of the Caesars' line, an end he says was foretold by signs. An eagle once dropped a hen holding a sprig of laurel into Livia's lap at her villa at Veii. The hen reared so many chickens that the place was still called the Villa of the Hens.

Laurels from that grove supplied the Caesars' triumphal crowns, and each emperor planted a new tree after a triumph. In Nero's last year the whole plantation withered to the roots and the hens died. Suetonius uses omens to mark the end of one dynasty and the brief opening of Galba's.

un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
Background opens the privacy part of the United Nations manual on computer crime, printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. It sets the scene in a few strokes. For solid goods, law guards the owner's stake. For facts, law must also weigh the people the facts describe.

Before computers, that second stake won scant cover. Libel law was nearly the whole shield. From the 1970s on, machines made it cheap to gather, store, match, and send vast files on a person. Fresh threats to privacy came with that power. States replied with office rules, civil suits, and some new crimes. World bodies then pushed for a shared line, as the next parts show.
